text.p: Ousted Afghan military chief Ahmad Shah Masood sent his fighters into action against the Islamic Taleban militia in a town behind the front lines on Saturday, putting scores of black-turbanned warriors to flight.

Masood forces also fired an estimated 300 shells and mortar bombs into Kabul's main airbase of Bagram 50 km (30 miles) north of the capital overnight and the Taleban responded with bombing raids by two MiG-21s, witnesses said.
It was not clear what damage was done by the MiGs or in the overnight shelling.

On Saturday, Masood struck Charikar, a mainly Tajik town a 30-minute drive from the Taleban front-line headquarters at Jabal-os-Siraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains which divide Afghanistan.
Taleban guards refused to talk about fighting that appeared to be going on in Charikar, ordering journalists to leave.
Journalists saw a convoy of Taleban trucks and pick-ups, along with a mobile rocket launcher truck, drive round a Taleban roadblock and speed off towards Kabul.

On Friday, the Taleban faced its worst day of setbacks as fighters loyal to Masood, military chief in the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, launched guerrilla attacks on supply lines north of Kabul, witnesses said.

Acting Taleban information minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told Reuters correspodent Jeremy Wagstaff his forces had suppressed insurgents and still held all towns on the plains north of the capital, including Bagram airbase, as well as the main highway.
"We are of the belief that with the aid of God no force can stop us in carrying out this work," he said.
"Our operation in the north of Kabul is against bandits and those forces which destroyed Afghanistan, looted the treasury and defamed Jihad (Holy War) and Islam."

On Friday local commanders spurred on by Masood cut a vital highway running from Kabul to the Taleban's northern frontline against Masood and militia chief Abdul Rashid Dostum, employing hit-and-run tactics the Taleban have not faced before.

The Taleban, which swept from the south to take Kabul a fortnight ago after overrunning much of the country, have found their supply lines under attack from small well-armed units using the guerrilla tactics perfected by Masood in his successful strikes on Soviet forces in the 1980s.

Dostum has yet to commit his well-equipped forces to the conflict but signed an agreement on Thursday with Masood and another local militia commander, Karim Khalili, pledging to support each other if attacked.

Mutaqi said he doubted Dostum would join Masood's forces but the Taleban were ready if he did. Any alliance between Dostum and Masood "will not affect the Taleban's resoluteness or decisiveness in the operations out of Kabul", he declared.
"We have not made any efforts so far to fight Khalili or Dostum, and I hope they will realise this. We are sure that General Dostum's forces or troops will not support Masood."

General Abdul Majid Ruzi, one of Dostum's commanders, told Reuters correspondent Kurt Schork in the Salang Pass: "Our relations with Masood's troops are correct but we have no orders from General Dostum to get involved in their fight.
"It would be better to solve this peacefully with negotiation. But if the order comes, we are ready."

Masood emerged earlier this week from his native Panjsher Valley some 80 km (50 miles) north of Kabul where he had been holed up since the Taleban takeover, to strike at Taleban positions north of Jabal-os-Siraj in fierce fighting.
Afghan watchers said the fate of the Taleban, the latest in a line of Afghan governments under siege, now depended on how fast they could adapt their tactics to the new situation.

Masood commanders said on Friday their forces may launch assaults on Jabal-os-Siraj, a key town at a fork in the road leading to Salang in the north, the Panjsher in the east, Kabul to the south, and Charikar, halfway along the Kabul highway.
Mutaqi said on Saturday all these towns were still held by Taleban forces.

The Taleban, applauded by some Afghans for the security they brought to areas under their control, said on Friday they had imposed a 9 p.m.-5 a.m. curfew on the capital, particularly for "journalists who make wrong reports".

The Taleban have reacted harshly to what they say is a hostile campaign by western media and governments against its movement, a campaign they say is driven by misunderstandings of its Islamic rules and journalists' abuse of their hospitality.
Mutaki also said it would be "disloyal" of the United Nations if the world body failed to recognise the Islamic movement's administration in Kabul, saying it represented the Afghan people.
A General Assembly committee on Friday deferred a decision on the credentials of Afghanistan's U.N. delegation, leaving in place representatives of ousted president Rabbani.
